Laceration

/lass-uh-RAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Laceration means a deep cut or tear in flesh.

Laceration means a deep cut or tear in flesh. The chef's knife slipped, leaving a laceration across her palm that needed immediate attention.

Worked Example

Halfway up the ridge, Dana's foot slipped and her forearm dragged across a sharp flake of granite. The rock tore through her sleeve and opened the skin below. At the trailhead clinic, the doctor irrigated the wound, then closed the laceration with eight stitches. She would climb again, but the scar would stay.

The torn-open wound that needed stitches — not a bruise or a light scrape — is what makes Dana's injury a laceration.

How Laceration Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

gash

gash: a long, deep cut

Antonyms

scratch

scratch: a light mark on the surface of the skin

graze

graze: a shallow scrape that barely breaks the skin

How Strong Is It? — nick → laceration → mutilation

nick vs. laceration

nick vs. laceration: A nick is a tiny, shallow cut that barely bleeds — far less serious than a laceration.

mutilation vs. laceration

mutilation vs. laceration: Mutilation is far more extreme than a laceration: severe, disfiguring damage to the body.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — lacer-

Root — lacer-: to tear (Latin lacerare)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: the act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Laceration comes from Latin lacerare, 'to tear to pieces,' plus the noun ending -ation: 'the result of tearing.' The verb lacerate survives in English with both a literal sense (torn flesh) and a figurative one (a review that tears a book apart). Don't be fooled by look-alikes such as lacquer or lackluster — they come from entirely different roots.

Use the root in a new word: lacerate

Use the root in a new word: lacerate: Critics can lacerate a film in their reviews — tearing it apart verbally — from the same Latin root lacerare, 'to tear.'

Root Check

Word Choice

clinical, medical

Laceration is the word doctors and first responders use for a cut or tear in flesh. Keep it apart from grievous (another word in this unit): a laceration is one specific physical injury, while grievous describes how severe any harm is — a laceration can be grievous, but grievous harm need not involve a cut at all.
